orgs.name: Karatay Madrasa
orgs.summary: A Seljuk madrasa in Konya, built in 1251. Its dome and its entrance hall carry some of the finest cut-tile mosaic of the 13th century.

orgs.name: Le Viandier
orgs.summary: A French cookbook of recipes for the royal and noble table. The oldest copies date from about 1300, and Taillevent widened the text. It was one of the first printed cookbooks.

orgs.name: Veneranda Fabbrica del Duomo di Milano
orgs.summary: The works office that builds and keeps Milan Cathedral. Its masons and stone workshops made the Gothic cathedral over centuries and still keep it.

orgs.name: Koberger printing house
orgs.summary: Anton Koberger opened the first printing house of Nuremberg and made it the largest publisher in Germany. It printed the Nuremberg Chronicle of 1493, with woodcuts from the Wolgemut workshop.

orgs.name: Court of Maximilian I
orgs.summary: The court of the king and emperor that paid for large woodcut projects. Hans Burgkmair cut portraits and book images for it, some as chiaroscuro woodcuts.

orgs.name: Aldine Press
orgs.summary: The press of Aldus Manutius. Its roman type, cut by Francesco Griffo, is the model of the Garalde old-style serif.

orgs.name: Aux Quatre Vents
orgs.summary: Hieronymus Cock and Volcxken Diericx founded this Antwerp print house. It issued more than 1,100 prints by 1570 and split the work into design, engraving and sale.

orgs.name: Accademia delle Arti del Disegno
orgs.summary: An academy of artists that Cosimo I de' Medici founded under the influence of Giorgio Vasari. It trained the painters of the late Renaissance court.

orgs.name: Opera dell'arte del cucinare
orgs.summary: A cookbook of six books by Scappi, with about 1,000 recipes and plates of the tools and the kitchen. It shows the first known picture of a fork.

orgs.name: Accademia di San Luca
orgs.summary: An academy of artists in Rome. It trained painters and architects, and Roman Baroque masters led it.

orgs.name: Raku family kiln
orgs.summary: The workshop of the Raku family in Kyoto. Chōjirō started it about 1580, and each head of the family makes black and red tea bowls to this day.

orgs.name: Rubenshuis
orgs.summary: The house and workshop of Peter Paul Rubens. Assistants and pupils painted large altarpieces here from his sketches.

orgs.name: Arita kilns
orgs.summary: The porcelain town of Kyushu where Japanese porcelain began in the early 17th century. Its kilns made Kakiemon and Imari ware for the home market and for Dutch export.

orgs.name: Ten Bamboo Studio
orgs.summary: The workshop of Hu Zhengyan in Nanjing. It made colour albums and embossed letter paper from small jigsaw blocks. Hu ran it from about 1619, and it went on into the Qing period.

orgs.name: Clement de Jonghe print shop
orgs.summary: An Amsterdam print shop that Clement de Jonghe ran from 1643 to 1677. It held more than 60,000 prints and many of the etched plates of Rembrandt.

orgs.name: Académie royale de peinture et de sculpture
orgs.summary: The royal academy of painting and sculpture in France. It trained the painters of the court and set the rules of taste for the Salon.

orgs.name: École des Beaux-Arts
orgs.summary: The state school of fine arts in Paris. Its architecture course taught axial plans and classical composition to students from many countries.

orgs.name: Le Cuisinier françois
orgs.summary: A French cookbook by La Varenne. It sets down the roux, the bouquet garni and the stock base, and went through many editions.

source.title: Wikipedia: François Pierre de La Varenne

orgs.name: De Porceleyne Fles
orgs.summary: A Delft pottery that started in 1653 and still makes tin-glazed and blue-painted ware. It is the last of the 17th-century Delft potteries.

orgs.name: Gobelins Manufactory
orgs.summary: The royal tapestry and furniture works of France. Colbert bought the site for Louis XIV in 1662. Charles Le Brun directed it from 1663.

orgs.name: Paris Salon
orgs.summary: The official art exhibition of the French Academy. For two centuries a painting had to succeed here to make a name, and each new school fought for its walls.

orgs.name: Académie royale d'architecture
orgs.summary: The royal academy of architecture in France. It taught the classical orders and sent its best students to study in Rome.

orgs.name: Meissen manufactory
orgs.summary: The first European maker of hard-paste porcelain. It started in 1710 under Augustus the Strong and made figures after the models of its chief modellers.

orgs.name: Rörstrand
orgs.summary: A Swedish pottery that started in Stockholm in 1726. From the 1760s it was a leading maker of tiled stoves for Swedish homes.

orgs.name: Society of Dilettanti
orgs.summary: A club of gentlemen who studied Greek and Roman art. It paid for the survey books of ancient buildings that architects then copied.

orgs.name: Blancpain watch manufacture
orgs.summary: The Swiss watch maker that made the Fifty Fathoms of 1953, one of the first modern diver's watches, to the drawing of two French divers.

orgs.name: Sèvres manufactory
orgs.summary: The French royal porcelain works. It started at Vincennes in 1740, moved to Sèvres in 1756 and made unglazed biscuit figures from 1751.

orgs.name: University of Pennsylvania
orgs.summary: The university that backed the Animal Locomotion study of Eadweard Muybridge. It published the 781 plates in 1887, printed as collotypes.

orgs.name: State Porcelain Factory, Petrograd
orgs.summary: The former Imperial Porcelain Factory, which the Soviet state took over in 1918. In the 1920s it made propaganda plates and, from 1923, the Suprematist tea ware.

orgs.name: Boydell print publishing
orgs.summary: John Boydell started as an engraver in London and became a large print publisher. His firm sold English engravings and mezzotints across Europe.

orgs.name: Bow Porcelain Factory
orgs.summary: A London factory that made soft-paste porcelain with bone ash from about 1747. It sold blue-and-white and enamelled tea ware at a low price.

orgs.name: Encyclopédie of Diderot and d'Alembert
orgs.summary: The French encyclopaedia of the Enlightenment. Its volumes of plates show the trades of the day, among them the stay-maker at his bench.

orgs.name: Soho Manufactory
orgs.summary: An early factory of Matthew Boulton. Its workers made buttons, buckles and small metal goods, with cut steel ornaments among them, by a division of labour.

orgs.name: Royal Academy of Arts
orgs.summary: The British academy of art, with an annual summer exhibition. Francesco Bartolozzi was a founder member, and stipple prints hung there.

orgs.name: Etruria Works
orgs.summary: The factory and the village that Josiah Wedgwood built in 1769. It made creamware, pearlware and jasperware with division of labour.

orgs.name: Spode works
orgs.summary: The Staffordshire pottery that Josiah Spode founded in 1770. It made printed blue-and-white earthenware and, later, bone china.

orgs.name: Kunstakademie Düsseldorf
orgs.summary: The art academy of Düsseldorf. Bernd and Hilla Becher taught photography here to the students of the Düsseldorf School.

orgs.name: Tsutaya
orgs.summary: The publishing house of Tsutaya Jūzaburō in Edo. It published woodblock prints by Utamaro, Sharaku and other masters.

orgs.name: Breguet watchmaking house
orgs.summary: The watchmaking house that Abraham-Louis Breguet opened in Paris in 1775. It made the thin, clear and exact watches of the classical Breguet style.

orgs.name: Galerie des modes et costumes français
orgs.summary: A series of engraved fashion plates of Paris dress, sold in sets to the court and the towns. It shows the Rococo gown and its change to plainer lines.

orgs.name: Calcografía Nacional
orgs.summary: The Spanish state print house in Madrid. It keeps the copper plates of Goya, with the plates of Los Caprichos, and it still prints from them.

orgs.name: Minton
orgs.summary: An English pottery that Thomas Minton started in 1793. Under Herbert Minton it became the leading maker of encaustic floor tiles.

orgs.name: Norton Pottery, Bennington
orgs.summary: A stoneware pottery that Captain John Norton started in 1793. It made salt-glazed crocks, jugs and churns with cobalt decoration for the farms of New England.

orgs.name: Journal des Dames et des Modes
orgs.summary: The Paris fashion journal that showed the new high-waisted dress of the Directory and the Empire in hand-coloured plates.

orgs.name: Fann Street Foundry
orgs.summary: A London type foundry. Robert Thorne cut early fat face types here.

orgs.name: Henry Poole and Co
orgs.summary: A London tailor that moved to Savile Row in 1846 and grew into its leading house. It cut and fitted coats by hand for the court and the clubs.

orgs.name: Doulton Lambeth
orgs.summary: A pottery at Lambeth that began in 1815. It made salt-glazed stoneware, drain pipes, sanitary ware, sinks and electrical insulators.

orgs.name: Duravit
orgs.summary: A German maker of sanitary ceramics that began in 1817 in the Black Forest. In 1994 it launched a range that Philippe Starck designed.

orgs.name: Brooks Brothers
orgs.summary: An American clothier that sold the unpadded sack jacket and the oxford button-down shirt. Its Madison Avenue store dressed the Ivy League man.

orgs.name: Expedition for the Preparation of State Papers
orgs.summary: The Russian state printing works for banknotes, bonds and stamps. It also printed colour books, among them Bilibin's fairy-tale series. Goznak took over its work in 1919.

orgs.name: Perkins, Bacon & Co
orgs.summary: A London printer of bank notes and stamps. It used steel plates and fine machine-made line work, and it printed the Penny Black in 1840.

orgs.name: Le Figaro
orgs.summary: A French daily newspaper. It printed the Symbolist manifesto in 1886 and the Futurist manifesto in 1909.

orgs.name: Le Cuisinier parisien
orgs.summary: A cookbook by Carême on the grand sauces, the stocks and the dressing of large dishes for the table of a great house.

orgs.name: Le Charivari
orgs.summary: A daily illustrated paper of caricature and satire. Honoré Daumier drew most of his lithographs for it.

orgs.name: Longines watch factory
orgs.summary: The Swiss watch factory that made the Hour Angle watch of 1931 for pilots, to the design of Weems and Lindbergh.

orgs.name: Bauer Type Foundry
orgs.summary: A German type foundry. It released Futura in 1927, the model of the geometric sans.

orgs.name: Duke University
orgs.summary: A university in North Carolina. Two of its graduate students planned Usenet there in 1979.

orgs.name: Dalziel Brothers
orgs.summary: A Victorian firm of wood engravers. It cut the blocks for many illustrators, among them Millais, Tenniel and Rossetti, until photographic processes took over c. 1880.

orgs.name: Glasgow Pottery (J. and M. P. Bell)
orgs.summary: A large Scottish pottery that made cheap sponged and printed earthenware for the home market and for export to North America.

orgs.name: Imprimerie Chaix
orgs.summary: A Paris printing works that Napoléon Chaix founded. From 1881 it printed the colour posters of Jules Chéret, its artistic director. It merged with Desfossé-Néogravure in 1965, and the Saint-Ouen works were sold in 1981.

orgs.name: Architectural Association School of Architecture
orgs.summary: An independent school of architecture. Its teachers in the 1970s included the first deconstructivists, and its research lab taught parametric design.

orgs.name: Cartier jewellery house
orgs.summary: The Paris jeweller that made early wristwatches for men and, from 1917, the Tank. Its shapes carried the wristwatch into Art Deco design.

orgs.name: Pre-Raphaelite Brotherhood
orgs.summary: Seven young British artists and writers who met in London in 1848. They wanted bright, detailed pictures drawn from nature and from serious subjects, and they rejected the soft manner of the Academy.

statement.text: Paint what you see in nature, in clear colour and fine detail, on subjects that carry a moral weight, and leave the habits of the Academy.

moves.text: Seven men formed the Brotherhood at the house of the parents of Millais in London.
The Brotherhood printed four issues of its journal The Germ between January and April.
The original Brotherhood had almost stopped by this year, after about five years.

orgs.name: John Lobb bootmaker
orgs.summary: The bespoke bootmaker that John Lobb founded in 1849. It makes welted shoes and boots on a last carved for each client.

orgs.name: Waltham Watch Company
orgs.summary: The American firm that made about 40 million watches and other timepieces from 1850 to 1957. Its machines cut parts that fit any watch of the same model.

orgs.name: Corning Glass Works
orgs.summary: An American glass maker. Its research laboratory made the first glass-ceramic in 1953, and the firm sold glass-ceramic cookware from 1958.

orgs.name: Dar al-Fonun
orgs.summary: A polytechnic school that the chancellor Amir Kabir founded in Tehran. Sources say that it had a lithographic press for teaching texts.

orgs.name: Great Exhibition
orgs.summary: The first world's fair, in the Crystal Palace. It showed the ornate manufactured furniture and goods of the Victorian age.

orgs.name: Bausch & Lomb optical works
orgs.summary: The optical firm of two German emigrants in Rochester. In 1937 it launched sun glasses with a thin metal frame and a large teardrop lens for pilots.

orgs.name: Levi Strauss and Company
orgs.summary: The dry goods house of Levi Strauss. From 1873 its factory made the riveted waist overall in denim and duck under a patent that Strauss shared with Jacob Davis.

orgs.name: Zsolnay manufactory
orgs.summary: A ceramics factory in Pécs that began in 1853. It made pyrogranite tiles, relief panels and eosin glazes for the roofs and facades of Hungarian Secession buildings.

orgs.name: Louis Vuitton trunk-maker's shop
orgs.summary: The shop that Louis Vuitton opened in Paris in 1854. It sold flat-topped trunks in coated canvas, built in a workshop at Asnières from 1859.

orgs.name: Burberry outfitters
orgs.summary: The outfitters of Thomas Burberry. They made gabardine in 1879 and sold the officer's trench coat and the windproof smock of the Everest parties.

orgs.name: Alpine Club
orgs.summary: The first mountaineering club of the world. Its members and its expedition committees planned the Everest parties of the 1920s.

orgs.name: H. Berthold AG
orgs.summary: A German type foundry. It released Akzidenz-Grotesk, the grotesque that Swiss designers later took up.

orgs.name: House of Worth
orgs.summary: The Paris couture house of Charles Frederick Worth. It set the shape of the crinoline and the bustle each season and fitted each gown by toile.

orgs.name: Heuer watch workshop
orgs.summary: The Swiss workshop that made stopwatches and chronographs for sport and, from the 1960s, the Carrera and the Monaco for drivers.

orgs.name: Morris & Co.
orgs.summary: The decorating firm of William Morris. It made and sold wallpaper, textiles, stained glass and furniture for Victorian and Arts and Crafts homes.

orgs.name: Bureau of Engraving and Printing
orgs.summary: The United States office that engraves and prints paper money. Its notes use fine line engraving in intaglio ink.

orgs.name: Salon des Refusés
orgs.summary: An official show of the works that the jury of the Paris Salon rejected in 1863. It put the new painting of modern life in front of a large public.

orgs.name: T. G. Green and Co.
orgs.summary: A pottery firm that Thomas Goodwin Green began in 1864 in Boston, Lincolnshire. Its works at Church Gresley made kitchen ware with blue bands from 1924, and the range gained the name Cornishware.

orgs.name: Caroline Reboux millinery house
orgs.summary: The hat house that Caroline Reboux opened in Paris in 1865. It made trimmed hats to order for the women of Paris.

orgs.name: Harper's Bazaar
orgs.summary: A fashion magazine. It printed the photographs of Richard Avedon and used Didot type for its name.

orgs.name: Peredvizhniki
orgs.summary: A society of Russian realist painters. It sent its shows by train to many towns, so that people outside the capital could see them. It was a free group, apart from the Academy.

statement.text: Take art out of the capital and the Academy, and show Russian life to Russian people in towns across the empire.

moves.text: The painters formed the Society for Travelling Art Exhibitions.
The first of 48 travelling exhibitions opened.
The last travelling exhibition took place.

orgs.name: Homer Laughlin China Company
orgs.summary: The American pottery that made Fiesta from 1936. It sold plain, strong earthenware in solid colours as open stock.

orgs.name: Tokyo National Museum
orgs.summary: The oldest national museum of Japan. It holds the flame-style Jōmon vessels, and Okamoto Tarō studied them there before he wrote his essay of 1952.

orgs.name: William De Morgan pottery
orgs.summary: The pottery of William De Morgan, first in Chelsea and then at Sands End in Fulham. It made tiles and vases in lustre and bright Persian colours.

orgs.name: Arabia factory
orgs.summary: The Helsinki ceramics factory with an art department. Its designers made plain, stackable services for daily use.

orgs.name: Kohler Co.
orgs.summary: A Wisconsin maker of baths, basins and WCs that began in 1873. It sold sanitary fixtures in colour, as a matched set.

orgs.name: Audemars Piguet watch workshop
orgs.summary: The Swiss workshop that made the Royal Oak of 1972, the first luxury sports watch in steel.

orgs.name: Coopers, Inc.
orgs.summary: A knitwear maker founded in 1876 in St Joseph, Michigan, later of Kenosha. It launched the Y-front brief in Chicago on 19 January 1935.

orgs.name: Sytin publishing house
orgs.summary: A Moscow printing and publishing firm that Ivan Sytin built from a small lithographic shop. It printed popular sheets, calendars and books in very large runs.

orgs.name: Hatch Show Print
orgs.summary: A letterpress shop in Nashville that the Hatch brothers founded. It prints concert posters from hand-cut wood blocks and old wood type.

orgs.name: Steubenville Pottery
orgs.summary: The Ohio pottery that made American Modern for Russel Wright. It sold the line in large numbers to department stores.

orgs.name: Hamilton Manufacturing Company
orgs.summary: The largest American maker of wood type. Printers used its heavy slab and fat face letters on posters.

orgs.name: Rookwood Pottery
orgs.summary: A pottery in Cincinnati that Maria Longworth Nichols founded in 1880. Its artists painted slip under a clear glaze, and the Standard glaze line made it famous.

orgs.name: Royal Society of Painter-Printmakers
orgs.summary: A British society of printmakers that started as the Society of Painter-Etchers. It holds exhibitions of etching, drypoint and other intaglio prints.

orgs.name: Seiko watch workshop
orgs.summary: The Japanese watch maker that sold the first quartz wristwatch, the Astron, on 25 December 1969.

orgs.name: Benz & Cie
orgs.summary: The works that Karl Benz founded in 1883. It built the Patent-Motorwagen and, from 1894, the Velo, the first car made in series.

orgs.name: Academy of Fine Arts, Istanbul
orgs.summary: The Ottoman school of fine arts (Sanayi-i Nefise Mektebi), now a state academy. Necmeddin Okyay taught ebru there.

orgs.name: Art Workers' Guild
orgs.summary: A guild of architects, artists and craftsmen. Its members met to join the arts again, and it gave the Arts and Crafts movement a home.

orgs.name: Salon des Indépendants
orgs.summary: An annual show without a jury. Seurat and Signac showed their dot paintings here, and the Cubists had a room here in 1911.

orgs.name: Linotype
orgs.summary: A maker of typesetting machines and type. It sold Helvetica, Frutiger and the formal script Snell Roundhand.

orgs.name: AEG
orgs.summary: German electrical firm. It hired Peter Behrens in 1907 as artistic consultant for its buildings, products and graphics.

orgs.name: Monotype
orgs.summary: A maker of typesetting machines and type. It released Gill Sans and revivals of Baskerville and other book faces.

orgs.name: Guild of Handicraft
orgs.summary: The craft guild that C. R. Ashbee founded. Its members made silver, enamel and gem jewels by hand and sold them in small runs.

orgs.name: Les Nabis
orgs.summary: Young painters from the Académie Julian in Paris who took Gauguin as their guide. They made flat, decorative pictures in rich colour, and they worked also on posters, prints, stage sets and book art.

statement.text: A picture is first a flat surface covered with colours in an order, before it is a horse, a nude or a story.
statement.title: Denis, Definition of Neo-traditionalism

moves.text: The linguist Auguste Cazalis gave the young painters the name Nabis, from a Hebrew word for prophets.
The group showed at the Maison de l'Art Nouveau of Siegfried Bing.
The Nabis held their last group show at the Galerie Bernheim and then went separate ways.

orgs.name: Guastavino Fireproof Construction Company
orgs.summary: A New York building firm that Rafael Guastavino started in 1889. It made thin tile vaults and tile linings for stations and halls.

orgs.name: Savoy Hotel
orgs.summary: A London hotel with electric light and its own restaurant kitchen. Escoffier and Ritz ran it from 1890 to 1897.

orgs.name: Kelmscott Press
orgs.summary: A private press that William Morris started to print books by hand in the manner of the early printers. It cut its own gothic types, Troy and Chaucer, after the letters of the first printed books.

orgs.name: Pilkington's Tile and Pottery Company
orgs.summary: A tile works near Manchester that started in 1891. It made moulded and glazed tiles in the Art Nouveau taste, for hearths, shops and halls.

orgs.name: Salon de la Rose + Croix
orgs.summary: A series of six art salons that Joséphin Péladan held. It showed mystic and Symbolist painting.

orgs.name: Vogue
orgs.summary: A fashion magazine. It commissions fashion photographs and sets its name in a high-contrast Didone type.

orgs.name: Ravi Varma Press
orgs.summary: A lithographic press that Raja Ravi Varma founded. It printed oleographs of his paintings of gods and legends for a mass market.

orgs.name: Le Cordon Bleu
orgs.summary: A cookery school in Paris that taught the classic French kitchen to home cooks and to professionals from abroad.

orgs.name: Maison de l'Art Nouveau
orgs.summary: The gallery of the dealer Siegfried Bing. It sold furniture, glass and rooms by new designers, and its name became the name of the style.

orgs.name: The Architectural Review
orgs.summary: A monthly architecture magazine. In 1955 it printed the essay that named the New Brutalism, and it published the work of the Smithsons.

orgs.name: House Beautiful
orgs.summary: An American interior design magazine. In 2019 it made the name grandmillennial popular for the young taste for chintz, ruffles and old pieces.

orgs.name: Jugend
orgs.summary: An illustrated weekly for art and life. Its covers and title lettering spread the German form of Art Nouveau, which took the name Jugendstil from it.

orgs.name: Mir iskusstva
orgs.summary: A circle of Russian artists and writers and its journal. The journal ran from 1899 to 1904, and the group met again from 1910 to 1924. It made the book page into an art form.

orgs.name: Paris Motor Show
orgs.summary: The motor show that opened in Paris in 1898. Makers and coachbuilders showed their new cars and bodies there each year.

orgs.name: Ver Sacrum
orgs.summary: The magazine of the Vienna Secession. Each issue set text, drawings and the monograms of its artists in a strict square page.

orgs.name: Detroit auto show
orgs.summary: The motor show that first opened in Detroit in 1899. In 1994 the Concept One was shown there and began the trend of the revived car.

orgs.name: Doves Press
orgs.summary: A private press in Hammersmith that printed in one typeface, the Doves Type. Its best-known book is the Doves Bible of 1902 to 1904.

orgs.name: Exposition Universelle of 1900
orgs.summary: A world's fair in Paris at the turn of the century. Art Nouveau buildings, rooms and metro entrances were on show, and the Finnish pavilion had frescoes of national myths.

orgs.name: Le Corset: Étude physiologique et pratique
orgs.summary: The book of 1900 by Inès Gaches-Sarraute. It sets out the health corset with a straight front and argues for it on the grounds of anatomy and hygiene.

orgs.name: Park Güell works
orgs.summary: The building site of Park Güell in Barcelona, which ran from 1900 to 1914. Masons set broken tile and china on its benches, roofs and walls.

orgs.name: Galerie B. Weill
orgs.summary: The gallery of Berthe Weill, opened on 1 December 1901 as a place for the young. It showed the Fauves in 1908 and 1909.

orgs.name: R. Griggs and Co.
orgs.summary: The Northamptonshire boot factory. In 1960 it took the licence for the air-cushioned sole and made the eight-eye boot.

orgs.name: Camera Work
orgs.summary: A quarterly of photography that Alfred Stieglitz edited and published, with fine photogravure plates. It argued for photography as a fine art.

orgs.name: Salon d'Automne
orgs.summary: An autumn art show in Paris. A critic called the painters of one room in 1905 wild beasts, and Fauvism got its name.

orgs.name: Wiener Werkstätte
orgs.summary: Viennese workshop of artists and craftspeople. It began in 1903 with money from Fritz Waerndorfer and closed in 1932.

orgs.name: Die Brücke
orgs.summary: A group of four architecture students in Dresden who became painters. They worked in raw, strong colour, printed woodcuts, and lived and worked together. In 1911 they moved to Berlin. They started German Expressionism.

statement.text: Young people who carry the future call for freedom of life and of action against the older, settled powers.
statement.title: Programm der Brücke

moves.text: Four students founded the group in Dresden.
Kirchner cut the programme of the group in a woodcut.
The Chronik der Brücke of Kirchner caused a break, and the group dissolved.

orgs.name: Van Cleef & Arpels workshop
orgs.summary: The jewellery house that Alfred Van Cleef and Salomon Arpels opened in Paris in 1906. Its workshop made the minaudière, a rigid evening case, in 1933.

orgs.name: Galerie Kahnweiler
orgs.summary: The gallery of the dealer Daniel-Henry Kahnweiler. He bought and sold the work of Picasso and Braque as they made Cubism.

orgs.name: Mondadori
orgs.summary: An Italian publishing house. Its crime novels with yellow covers gave giallo its name.

orgs.name: Converse Rubber Shoe Company
orgs.summary: The rubber shoe factory that Marquis Converse opened in 1908. In 1917 it made the canvas All Star basketball shoe.

orgs.name: Harris Tweed Association
orgs.summary: The trade body of the Hebridean weavers. It set the Orb mark of 1909 for tweed that is hand-woven at home in the islands.

orgs.name: Neue Künstlervereinigung München
orgs.summary: A Munich society of avant-garde painters that grew from the salon of Marianne von Werefkin. Kandinsky was its first chairman. It broke over his abstract work, and the break gave rise to Der Blaue Reiter.

moves.text: The association was formed in Munich and entered in the register of associations on 10 May.
The first travelling show opened in December at the Moderne Galerie of Thannhauser.
The jury rejected Composition V of Kandinsky in December. He and Marc then formed Der Blaue Reiter.

orgs.name: Der Sturm
orgs.summary: A magazine and gallery of Herwarth Walden. It published and showed Expressionist art.

emblem.credit: Wikimedia Commons contributors; see the file page

orgs.name: Jack of Diamonds
orgs.summary: A Moscow society of painters that brought French Cubism, Cézanne and Russian folk art together. Its first show in 1910 caused a scandal. The radical members left in 1912.

statement.text: Join the structure of Cézanne with the colour of Russian folk art, and show the new French painters in Moscow.

moves.text: The first exhibition opened in Moscow on 10 December with 38 artists. Larionov chose the name.
Larionov, Goncharova and other radical members left and formed the Donkey's Tail.
The sixth exhibition ended in December, and the group dissolved.

orgs.name: Chanel couture house
orgs.summary: The Paris house that Gabrielle Chanel opened as a hat shop in 1910. In the 1920s it made the jersey chemise and the short black dress.

orgs.name: Der Blaue Reiter
orgs.summary: A short-lived group round Kandinsky and Marc in Munich. They put on two shows, published an almanac in 1912, and held that colour and form can carry the spirit of the work without a subject.

statement.text: Art of all peoples and times, and the work of children, belongs side by side, because each shows an inner need and not an outer look.
statement.title: Blaue Reiter Almanac

moves.text: The first exhibition opened on 18 December at the Moderne Galerie of Thannhauser, with 43 works by 14 artists.
Kandinsky and Marc published the Almanac.
A second show of black and white work opened at the gallery of Hans Goltz in Munich.
The group ended when the First World War began.

orgs.name: Donkey's Tail
orgs.summary: A Moscow group of the most radical painters who broke with the Jack of Diamonds. Larionov led it. It showed folk art and child-like pictures, and it ended with its last show in 1914. Larionov announced Rayonism at the Target show in 1913.

statement.text: Leave the careful Cézannism of the older Moscow painters, and take the lead from folk prints, signboards and Rayonist lines.

moves.text: The first main exhibition ran from 11 March to 8 April in the hall of the School of Painting, Sculpture and Architecture in Moscow.
The catalogue of the Target show announced Rayonism as the style of the group.
The last show, No. 4, opened in Moscow in March.

orgs.name: IBM
orgs.summary: A maker of office machines and computers. Its typewriters made Courier the common monospace.

orgs.name: Section d'Or
orgs.summary: A circle of Cubist painters who met in Puteaux and Courbevoie near Paris. Their name pointed to the golden section and to the long line of classical art. They held one large show in 1912.

statement.text: Cubism is part of the long French line of art that rests on number and proportion, and it is more than a Montmartre fashion.
statement.title: Du Cubisme

moves.text: The Cubist room at the Salon des Indépendants brought the circle to public notice.
Gleizes and Metzinger published Du Cubisme, and the group put out the review La Section d'Or.
The Salon de la Section d'Or opened on 9 October at the Galerie La Boétie in Paris, with more than 200 works.

orgs.name: Carrozzeria Bertone
orgs.summary: The coachbuilding works that Giovanni Bertone founded in 1912. In the 1960s and 1970s it built the wedge-shaped show cars of Marcello Gandini.

orgs.name: Gazette du Bon Ton
orgs.summary: A Paris fashion magazine for subscribers that Lucien Vogel founded. It showed couture designs in pochoir plates, coloured by hand through stencils.

orgs.name: Vionnet couture house
orgs.summary: The Paris house of Madeleine Vionnet. Its workroom draped each gown on a small doll and cut it on the bias.

orgs.name: Kurt Wolff Verlag
orgs.summary: A German publishing house. It published the photobook "Die Welt ist schön" of Albert Renger-Patzsch, a key book of New Objectivity photography.

orgs.name: Lacerba
orgs.summary: A Florentine review that published the Futurists and their manifestos in loud type.

orgs.name: Werkbund Exhibition Cologne 1914
orgs.summary: The show of the German Werkbund. It put industrial buildings, machines and factory-made objects next to craft work, and it made the work of the factory a subject of design.

orgs.name: De Stijl
orgs.summary: The magazine that Theo van Doesburg edited for the De Stijl group. It printed their theory of pure colour and the straight line.

orgs.name: Toto
orgs.summary: A Japanese sanitary ware maker that began in 1917 as Toyo Toki. It launched the Washlet, a toilet seat with a warm-water spray, in 1980.

orgs.name: UFA
orgs.summary: The large German film company of the Weimar years. Its studios made Metropolis and other films of German Expressionist cinema.

orgs.name: Ukrainian Academy of Arts
orgs.summary: An art school that opened in Kyiv in December 1917. Narbut was a professor and then rector there. In 1922 the authorities renamed it the Institute of Plastic Arts.

orgs.name: Arbeitsrat für Kunst
orgs.summary: A council of architects and artists after the First World War. Its members drew visionary crystal buildings and showed them in exhibitions.

statement.text: Art and the people must form one unity, and the arts must come together under the wings of a great architecture.
statement.title: Arbeitsrat für Kunst programme

moves.text: Artists and architects founded the council in Berlin after the war.
The council showed the Exhibition for Unknown Architects in Berlin.
The council ended its work.

orgs.name: Nihon Sosaku Hanga Kyokai
orgs.summary: The Japan Creative Print Association. Its members held shows of prints that the artists drew, cut and printed alone. It closed in 1931 and later came back as the Nihon Hanga Kyokai.

orgs.name: Otis Art Institute
orgs.summary: An art school in Los Angeles that opened in 1918. Peter Voulkos taught ceramics there from 1954 and trained a group of artists who made clay sculpture.

orgs.name: ROSTA
orgs.summary: The Russian Telegraph Agency of the early Soviet state. Its artists made the ROSTA Windows: stencilled news strips for shop windows. In 1925 TASS took over the agency.

orgs.name: Bauhaus
orgs.summary: A school of art, craft and design that joined the workshop to the studio. Its teachers and students set the forms of modern design, interiors and building.

orgs.name: Glass Chain
orgs.summary: A chain of letters among a small circle of architects and artists around Bruno Taut. Each member signed with a code name and sent drawings of crystal and glass buildings.

moves.text: Bruno Taut sent the first circular letter to a chosen circle of friends in November.
The letters stopped in December 1920.

orgs.name: Gerasimov Institute of Cinematography
orgs.summary: The first film school in the world. Lev Kuleshov ran a workshop here, and Sergei Eisenstein taught here.

orgs.name: Architectural Digest
orgs.summary: A magazine of interiors and houses. It published the homes of Hollywood stars and later the soft, curved rooms of new glamour.

orgs.name: Eddie Bauer sports shop
orgs.summary: The sports shop that Eddie Bauer opened in Seattle in 1920. In 1936 it sold the first quilted goose-down jacket.

orgs.name: Leach Pottery
orgs.summary: A pottery at St Ives in Cornwall that Bernard Leach and Shōji Hamada founded in 1920. It made high-fired stoneware in a Japanese climbing kiln and trained many studio potters.

orgs.name: UNOVIS
orgs.summary: A group of artists and students that Kazimir Malevich led. It spread Suprematism into design, print and teaching.

orgs.name: Braun
orgs.summary: A German maker of radios, record players and small appliances. Its design team under Dieter Rams made the calm, functional products that later shaped interface design.

orgs.name: Kinoks
orgs.summary: A Soviet group of film makers: Vertov, his wife Svilova and his brother Kaufman. They rejected the staged drama and wanted the camera to show life as it is, cut into a film.

statement.title: We: A Variant of a Manifesto
statement.text: The film maker drops the staged drama and the actor, and shows life caught by the camera, cut into a film with rhythm.

moves.text: Vertov, Svilova and Kaufman formed the group; the source calls the three the Council of Three.
The group began to print manifestos in avant-garde journals (1922 to 1923), among them LEF.
Svilova wrote an open letter to LEF to ask to join the Council of Three; scholars read it as a publicity stunt, as she already worked with the group.
Man with a Movie Camera came out, the best known work of the group.

orgs.name: Maidenform
orgs.summary: A maker of brassières founded in 1922 for the flapper years. It was run by Ida Rosenthal, and in the Second World War it turned its factories to pigeon vests and parachutes.

orgs.name: Herman Miller
orgs.summary: A furniture maker that worked with George Nelson, Charles and Ray Eames and Isamu Noguchi. It made modern furniture for homes and offices.

orgs.name: LEF
orgs.summary: A journal of the Soviet left front of the arts. Rodchenko made its covers with photomontage, diagonals and heavy type, the vocabulary that constructivist web pages take up.

orgs.name: La Pyramide
orgs.summary: A restaurant in Vienne on the road to the south. Fernand Point ran it from 1924 until 1955, and it trained a generation of French chefs.

orgs.name: La Révolution surréaliste
orgs.summary: The first magazine of the Surrealist group. It printed dreams, automatic writing and Surrealist paintings.

orgs.name: Svenskt Tenn
orgs.summary: A Stockholm interior design shop that Estrid Ericson founded. It sold pewter, furniture and prints in a light Swedish style.

orgs.name: International Exhibition of Modern Decorative and Industrial Arts
orgs.summary: A world's fair of decorative and industrial arts. Its pavilions and rooms showed the new luxury style that later got the name Art Deco from this show.

orgs.name: Grosvenor School of Modern Art
orgs.summary: A private art school in Pimlico. Claude Flight taught colour linocut there, and Cyril Power and Sybil Andrews learned and worked with him.

orgs.name: Fendi house
orgs.summary: A Roman house of fur and leather goods, opened in 1925 by Adele and Edoardo Fendi. In 1997 it launched the Baguette bag.

orgs.name: Der Ring
orgs.summary: A union of modern architects in Berlin. Its members wanted a new, functional way of building and a shared voice against the conservative architects of the city.

moves.text: Ten architects founded the group in Berlin.
Members of the group built houses at the Weissenhof Estate in Stuttgart.
The group dissolved under the Nazi government.

orgs.name: Weissenhof Estate
orgs.summary: A housing estate that the Deutscher Werkbund built as an exhibition. Seventeen architects made white, flat-roofed houses side by side.

orgs.name: CIAM
orgs.summary: A council of modern architects who met in congresses from 1928 to 1959. Its members wrote the rules for the functional city. A younger group, Team 10, broke its doctrine.

statement.text: Architecture is a social and economic act; the architect must plan for the whole of society, not only design buildings.
statement.title: La Sarraz Declaration

moves.text: Twenty-eight architects met at La Sarraz and founded the congress.

source.title: Wikipedia: International Congresses of Modern Architecture

moves.text: The fourth congress sailed to Athens and wrote the rules of the functional city; Le Corbusier edited them and published them in 1943 as the Athens Charter.

source.title: Wikipedia: International Congresses of Modern Architecture

moves.text: At the ninth congress in Aix-en-Provence the younger members attacked the doctrine of the functional city.
The congress dissolved at its last meeting in Otterlo.

source.title: Wikipedia: International Congresses of Modern Architecture

orgs.name: Eastern Color Printing
orgs.summary: A colour printer in Connecticut that published Famous Funnies, the first American comic book in the modern form. It printed comics for other publishers until 1973.

orgs.name: RKO Pictures
orgs.summary: A Hollywood studio of the studio era. It made classic Hollywood films and many low-key film noirs, with their publicity stills.

emblem.credit: Frank Ross productions Ltd. Rko Radio Pictures

orgs.name: Arts & Architecture
orgs.summary: A California magazine of art and building. Its Case Study House program built and published modern homes, with photos by Julius Shulman.

orgs.name: Pergamon Museum
orgs.summary: A museum in Berlin that opened in 1930. It shows the Ishtar Gate of Babylon, rebuilt from the glazed bricks that the German excavators dug up in the early 20th century.

orgs.name: Carrozzeria Pinin Farina
orgs.summary: The coachbuilding works that Battista Farina founded in 1930. It made the bodies of many Italian grand tourers by hand and in small series.

orgs.name: Stockholm Exhibition
orgs.summary: An exhibition of design and housing. Its light, glass pavilions brought functionalism to the Nordic countries.

orgs.name: Julien Levy Gallery
orgs.summary: A New York gallery. In 1932 it held the first show of the official Surrealist group in the city. It showed Dalí from 1933.

orgs.name: Group f/64
orgs.summary: The first show of Group f/64 at the M. H. de Young Museum. It showed sharp, straight prints against pictorialism.

orgs.name: Modern Architecture: International Exhibition
orgs.summary: A show at the Museum of Modern Art. Its catalogue named the International Style and showed the work of the European modernists to America.

orgs.name: Artek
orgs.summary: A furniture company that Alvar Aalto and three partners started to sell his bent birch furniture.

emblem.credit: Wikimedia Commons contributors; see the file page

orgs.name: Centro Sperimentale di Cinematografia
orgs.summary: The national film school of Italy. Several makers and writers of Italian neorealism studied or taught here.

orgs.name: WPA Federal Art Project
orgs.summary: US relief programme from 1935 to 1943. It paid up to 10,000 artists weekly wages, among them Jackson Pollock.

orgs.name: FSA Historical Section photography project
orgs.summary: US government photography project of 1935 to 1944 under Roy Stryker. It made about 250,000 images of rural poverty.

orgs.name: Japan Folk Crafts Museum
orgs.summary: A museum of everyday craft that Yanagi Soetsu founded to show and teach the beauty of plain, hand-made objects. It made the mingei idea known to makers and designers.

orgs.name: Life
orgs.summary: The weekly photo magazine that Henry Luce started in 1936 from an older humour magazine of the same name. It made the photo essay a main form of documentary photography.

orgs.name: Cinecittà
orgs.summary: A large film studio in Rome. Many Italian westerns of the 1960s were made in its studios.

orgs.name: Roger Vivier shoe house
orgs.summary: The shoe house that Roger Vivier opened in Paris in 1937. It made the thin-heeled court shoes of the 1950s for the couture houses.

orgs.name: New Bauhaus and School of Design, Chicago
orgs.summary: The school that László Moholy-Nagy opened in Chicago on the model of the Bauhaus. It taught design with a bench and a workshop, and Margaret De Patta studied there.

orgs.name: Taller de Gráfica Popular
orgs.summary: A workshop of printmakers that made leaflets, posters and portfolios in linocut and woodcut for workers, unions and the state.

orgs.name: Knoll
orgs.summary: A furniture maker that produced designs by Mies van der Rohe, Eero Saarinen and Marcel Breuer. Its planning unit set the look of the modern office.

orgs.name: Lu Xun Academy of Arts
orgs.summary: An art school that began in Yan'an in April 1938. It taught the woodcut to young artists. It still runs as the Lu Xun Academy of Fine Arts in Shenyang.

orgs.name: Madoura pottery
orgs.summary: A pottery in Vallauris that Suzanne and Georges Ramié ran. Picasso worked there from 1947, and the pottery fired and sold his editions.

orgs.name: Albion Mews studio
orgs.summary: The small studio of Lucie Rie in a former coach house in London. Hans Coper worked there from 1946 to 1958, and both potters made modernist studio ceramics there.

orgs.name: National Film Board of Canada
orgs.summary: The public film producer of Canada. Its unit for observational films made early direct cinema with light cameras.

orgs.name: 1939 New York World's Fair
orgs.summary: A world's fair of two seasons with the theme The World of Tomorrow. Its pavilions, cars and appliances showed streamlined shells to millions of visitors.

orgs.name: Art of This Century
orgs.summary: The gallery of Peggy Guggenheim. It gave Jackson Pollock his first solo show.

orgs.name: IKEA
orgs.summary: A Swedish furniture company. It sold light, plain, flat-packed furniture to homes around the world.

orgs.name: Exquisite Form
orgs.summary: A maker of foundation garments and brassières founded in 1945. In 1964 it made the No Bra of Rudi Gernreich, a soft bra without bone or lining.

orgs.name: Betty Parsons Gallery
orgs.summary: The gallery of the dealer Betty Parsons. It showed Pollock, Rothko and Newman when few dealers took them.

orgs.name: Cannes Film Festival
orgs.summary: An annual film festival with a juried competition. It gave prizes to neorealist, New Hollywood, Dogme 95 and slow-cinema films.

orgs.name: Christian Dior couture house
orgs.summary: The couture house that Christian Dior opened in 1946. Its ateliers cut, fitted and sewed the New Look by hand.

orgs.name: Riso Kagaku Corporation
orgs.summary: The Japanese company that makes the Risograph stencil duplicator. It also made Print Gocco, a small screen-print kit for the home.

orgs.name: Armet & Davis
orgs.summary: A Californian architecture firm that designed hundreds of coffee shops and diners. Its roadside buildings with flying roofs and big signs defined Googie.

moves.text: Louis Armet and Eldon Davis formed the firm.
The firm built Norms La Cienega in West Hollywood, with a sign and a roof made for drivers.

orgs.name: Magnum Photos
orgs.summary: A cooperative that its photographers own. Its members made documentary and street photography for magazines.

orgs.name: CoBrA
orgs.summary: A group of artists from Copenhagen, Brussels and Amsterdam, and the name comes from those three cities. They painted fast, with thick colour and the drawing of children, and they worked as one team.

statement.text: Make art together, from spontaneous play and from the people, and reject the theory and the taste of the Paris schools.
statement.title: La cause était entendue

moves.text: The founders met on 8 November at the Café Notre-Dame in Paris.
The International Experimental Art show opened at the Stedelijk Museum in Amsterdam in November. The press and the public attacked it.
The group dissolved after its second large show, in Liège.

orgs.name: Heath Ceramics
orgs.summary: A pottery that makes stoneware tableware in a studio and a factory. In 2006 it made a collection for a chef and her restaurant.

orgs.name: Sidney Janis Gallery
orgs.summary: A New York gallery. It gave Pollock the first of three solo shows in 1952 and held the New Realists show of 1962.

orgs.name: General Motors Motorama
orgs.summary: A travelling show of dream cars that General Motors ran from 1949 to 1961. It showed fins, glass roofs and chrome years before production.

orgs.name: Congress for Cultural Freedom
orgs.summary: Anti-communist cultural network founded in West Berlin in 1950. The CIA funded it until 1966.

orgs.name: Berlin International Film Festival
orgs.summary: An annual film festival with a juried competition. The symmetrical, planimetric film The Grand Budapest Hotel opened it in 2014.

orgs.name: Cahiers du cinéma
orgs.summary: A French film magazine. Its young critics argued that the director is the author of a film, and several of them went on to make the first films of the French New Wave.

statement.title: A Certain Tendency of the French Cinema
statement.text: Truffaut attacks the tradition of quality of the French studio film and asks for the director as author.

moves.text: Bazin, Doniol-Valcroze and Lo Duca founded the magazine.
Truffaut printed his attack on the tradition of quality.
The young critics round Rivette forced Rohmer out and put Rivette in as editor.
Le Monde bought the publisher.

orgs.name: Festival of Britain
orgs.summary: National festival of summer 1951. It gave a platform to the Contemporary style and to Good Design.

orgs.name: Aperture
orgs.summary: A publisher of photobooks and a magazine. It published colour work of Stephen Shore and other New Colour photographers.

orgs.name: Perspecta
orgs.summary: The architecture journal of the Yale School of Architecture. In 1983 it printed the essay that argued for a critical regionalism.

orgs.name: Ulm School of Design
orgs.summary: A school of design that taught system, grid and method. Its teachers worked with Braun and with corporate identity programs.

orgs.name: Team 10
orgs.summary: A loose group of younger architects who broke from CIAM. They wanted cities built from human relations, streets and thresholds, not from four fixed functions.

statement.text: Architects must plan from the ways people live and meet, and the cluster of human association must replace the four functions of the functional city.
statement.title: Doorn Manifesto

moves.text: The young members of CIAM IX in Aix-en-Provence put forward a new view of the city against the old doctrine.
The group met at Doorn and wrote a manifesto on human association.
The group held a first formal meeting at Bagnols-sur-Cèze.
The group ended after the death of Jaap Bakema.

orgs.name: Gutai Art Association
orgs.summary: A Japanese group led by Jiro Yoshihara. Its members painted with feet, mud and balls, and made shows in parks and on stage. The name means concrete: they let the matter speak.

statement.text: Art gives life to matter, so the artist leaves the paint, the mud and the metal to show their own nature.
statement.title: Gutai Art Manifesto

moves.text: Yoshihara founded the group in Ashiya.
The group held an open-air show in Ashiya Park.
The Gutai Art Manifesto appeared in the magazine Geijutsu Shincho in December.
Yoshihara died in February, and the members ended the group in March.

orgs.name: The Fillmore
orgs.summary: A music hall in San Francisco where Bill Graham started to book shows in 1965. Its weekly concert posters spread the psychedelic poster style.

orgs.name: Bazaar boutique
orgs.summary: The shop that Mary Quant and Alexander Plunket Greene opened on the King's Road. It sold short dresses and miniskirts to young Londoners.

orgs.name: documenta
orgs.summary: A large exhibition of contemporary art every five years. Its 1972 edition showed the American photorealists.

orgs.name: Bon Appétit
orgs.summary: An American food magazine. Its food photography sets the look of home cooking in print and online.

orgs.name: Graham Foundation
orgs.summary: Chicago foundation for architecture, founded in 1956. It backed Robert Venturi's book Complexity and Contradiction in Architecture.

orgs.name: Chermayeff & Geismar
orgs.summary: A New York design studio. It drew simple geometric symbols for banks, networks and museums.

orgs.name: Leo Castelli Gallery
orgs.summary: The gallery of the dealer Leo Castelli. It showed Pop Art and then Minimalism.

orgs.name: Situationist International
orgs.summary: A group of artists and writers led by Guy Debord. It joined three small avant-garde bodies, and it turned from art to a critique of city life and of the spectacle. Punk designers used its ideas later.

statement.text: Build situations, which are moments of life made on purpose, and fight the spectacle that turns life into an image.
statement.title: Report on the Construction of Situations

moves.text: The Lettrist International, the Imaginist Bauhaus and the London Psychogeographical Association merged at a meeting in Cosio di Arroscia in July.
The German group Spur was expelled in February. Later in the year the Scandinavian group of Jorgen Nash was also expelled.
Debord published The Society of the Spectacle.
The Situationist International dissolved.

orgs.name: Zero
orgs.summary: Two artists in Düsseldorf, Mack and Piene, who held evening shows in their studio. Uecker joined them in 1961. They worked with light, movement and empty fields of one colour, as a fresh start after the war.

statement.text: Zero is a zone of silence and of pure chance for a new beginning.

moves.text: Mack and Piene began to show work in their studio in Düsseldorf.
Motion in Vision, the first large Zero show with an international public, opened in Antwerp.

orgs.name: Neue Grafik
orgs.summary: A trilingual review of graphic design, set on a strict grid, that four Swiss designers edited. It made the case for the International Typographic Style.

orgs.name: W. L. Gore and Associates
orgs.summary: The firm of Wilbert and Robert Gore. It made the Gore-Tex membrane and, from 1976, laminated it to cloth for shells.

orgs.name: Archigram
orgs.summary: A group of six young London architects who published a magazine of cities as machines. They drew walking cities, plug-in frames and living pods, but built almost nothing.

statement.text: The city is a set of changing, plug-in parts, so the architect must draw it with the joy of pop machines and not with the stone of the past.
statement.title: Archigram magazine

moves.text: The group printed the first issue of the Archigram magazine.
The group showed the Living City exhibition at the ICA in London.
Peter Cook drew Plug-in City (1964 to 1966) and Ron Herron drew Walking City.
The group ended after the last issue and the last big commission.

orgs.name: Cinema Novo
orgs.summary: A Brazilian film movement of young directors who filmed poverty, the land and the state in a rough form. Its three phases ran from 1960 to 1972.

statement.title: Aesthetics of Hunger
statement.text: Rocha says that hunger is the root of Brazilian society, so a Brazilian film must show hunger and its violence with a rough form.

moves.text: The movement began; historians split it into three phases, 1960 to 1964, 1964 to 1968 and 1968 to 1972.
Black God, White Devil came out, and a military coup removed President Goulart.
Rocha wrote Aesthetics of Hunger.
A rival group, Cinema Marginal, rose against the third phase.

orgs.name: Fjällräven
orgs.summary: The Swedish maker of outdoor kit. Its waxed poly-cotton twill jackets and frame rucksacks set the plain, repairable look of Nordic trail wear.

orgs.name: Metabolists
orgs.summary: A Japanese group of young architects and a critic who saw the city as a living body. They drew cities of replaceable capsules on fixed cores, and showed them first in Tokyo in 1960.

statement.text: Cities and buildings grow and change like living things, so the architect must plan fixed cores with parts that people can replace.
statement.title: Metabolism: The Proposals for New Urbanism

moves.text: The group published its manifesto for the World Design Conference in Tokyo.
Tange master-planned the Expo 70 site in Osaka, and Kikutake and Kurokawa designed pavilions.

orgs.name: Sega
orgs.summary: A Japanese game and hardware company that made the Mega Drive and fast parallax side-scrollers.

orgs.name: Courrèges couture house
orgs.summary: The couture house that André Courrèges opened in 1961. It cut and sewed the white A-line dresses and flat boots of the Space Age collection.

orgs.name: Oberhausen Group
orgs.summary: Twenty-six young West German film makers who signed a short manifesto at the Oberhausen short film festival. They declared the old German film dead and asked for the freedom to make a new one.

statement.title: Oberhausen Manifesto
statement.text: The old film is dead, and the signatories say that they take the economic risk to make a new German film free of the industry and its interests.

moves.text: Twenty-six film makers read the manifesto at a press conference on 28 February at the Oberhausen festival.
The Interior Ministry created the Kuratorium junger deutscher Film, a fund for first features.
Kluge’s Abschied von gestern came out, one of the first films of the New German Cinema.
Reitz’s Mahlzeiten came out and won the prize for a first work at Venice.

orgs.name: Team 4
orgs.summary: A small architecture practice of Norman Foster, Richard Rogers and two partners. Its factory building at Swindon used light steel and glass in the way of the later high-tech.

orgs.name: Blue Ribbon Sports
orgs.summary: The running shoe company of Bill Bowerman and Phil Knight. It sold the first waffle-soled shoes before it took the name Nike.

orgs.name: elBulli
orgs.summary: A restaurant on Cala Montjoi in Catalonia, on a site bought in 1961 and open as a restaurant from 1964; under Ferran Adrià, its winter research workshop made foams, spheres and the deconstructed dish.

orgs.name: 1964 New York World's Fair
orgs.summary: A world's fair of two seasons with the theme of the space age. Its pavilions, rockets and futuristic rides showed the optimism of space-age design.

orgs.name: The Factory
orgs.summary: The studio of Andy Warhol. Assistants printed silkscreens there, and artists, actors and musicians met there.

orgs.name: Museu Nacional do Azulejo
orgs.summary: A national museum of the tile in the former Madre de Deus convent in Lisbon. It shows Portuguese tiles from the late 15th century to the present.

orgs.name: National Endowment for the Arts
orgs.summary: Independent US federal agency created by Congress in 1965. It gave fellowships to photographers.

orgs.name: Archizoom Associati
orgs.summary: A Florence group that mixed pop colour with a critique of the market. It drew No-Stop City, a city as one endless room, and made furniture for Poltronova.

moves.text: Archizoom and Superstudio held the Superarchitettura show in Pistoia.
The group designed the Superonda sofa for Poltronova.
The group ended its work.

orgs.name: Family Dog Productions
orgs.summary: A concert promoter in San Francisco that Chet Helms ran. Its dance concerts from 1966 to 1968 each had a new poster.

orgs.name: San Francisco Oracle
orgs.summary: An underground paper of the Haight-Ashbury scene. It printed rainbow inks over swirling art and lettering.

orgs.name: Superstudio
orgs.summary: A Florence group that drew the endless grid as a critique of consumer society. Its collages show one monument that wraps the whole earth.

statement.text: Architecture is an act of consumption that should become an endless, neutral grid so that people can live without objects.
statement.title: Superarchitettura

moves.text: Superstudio and Archizoom held the Superarchitettura show in Pistoia.
The group drew the Continuous Monument as a series of photomontages.
The group showed its work at the MoMA exhibition Italy: The New Domestic Landscape.
The group ended its joint work.

orgs.name: Funk exhibition, Berkeley
orgs.summary: A show of 1967 at the University Art Museum in Berkeley that gave the name Funk to the rude, hand-made work of California artists, with ceramics by Arneson and his circle.

orgs.name: L.A. Rebellion
orgs.summary: A group of African and African-American students at the UCLA film school. They made films on Black life as an answer to the Hollywood picture.

moves.text: Killer of Sheep came out.
Bush Mama came out.
Daughters of the Dust came out.

orgs.name: New Documents
orgs.summary: A photography show at the Museum of Modern Art. It showed street photographs by Garry Winogrand, Diane Arbus and Lee Friedlander.

orgs.name: Smithsonian Folklife Festival
orgs.summary: An annual festival of living culture. In 2015 it showed the urban art and music of Peru, with chicha posters.

orgs.name: Calvin Klein fashion house
orgs.summary: The fashion house that Calvin Klein founded in 1968. In the 1980s its underwear and jeans lines made the name on the waistband a mark of status.

orgs.name: Dziga Vertov Group
orgs.summary: A group of political film makers round Godard and Gorin. They made Marxist films with no single author, and they took the name of the Kinoks' leader.

statement.title: Make films politically
statement.text: The group does not make political films about a subject; it makes films in a political way, with no star and no single author.

moves.text: Godard and Gorin formed the group after May 1968.
Pravda and Wind from the East came out.
Struggles in Italy and Vladimir and Rosa came out.
Godard and Gorin made Tout va bien as a pair, and the group name went out of use.

orgs.name: Jil Sander fashion house
orgs.summary: The Hamburg house that Jil Sander began in 1968. It made plain clothes in fine cloth that set the line of 1990s minimalism.

orgs.name: Zanzibar Group
orgs.summary: A French group of young artists and film makers. Sylvina Boissonnas paid for their films. A critic called them the dandies of May 1968.

moves.text: The group began to make films with money from Sylvina Boissonnas.
The group ended when Boissonnas stopped her funds and turned to the feminist movement.

orgs.name: Comme des Garçons
orgs.summary: The label that Rei Kawakubo founded in Tokyo in 1969. Its 1981 Paris show brought the black, loose Japanese line to Europe.

orgs.name: Gault et Millau guide
orgs.summary: A French restaurant guide and monthly founded by Henri Gault and Christian Millau: the monthly Le Nouveau Guide began in 1969, the yearly guide book in 1972. It marks restaurants from 1 to 20 and in 1973 it printed the ten characteristics of nouvelle cuisine.

orgs.name: Golden Harvest
orgs.summary: A Hong Kong film company. It produced the films of Bruce Lee and Jackie Chan and the Hong Kong action of the 1970s and 1980s.

emblem.credit: Sindala at Dutch Wikipedia, converted to SVG by FireDragonValo

orgs.name: Nintendo R&D1
orgs.summary: The Nintendo hardware and game team that designed the Game Boy and its first games.

orgs.name: Chez Panisse
orgs.summary: A restaurant in Berkeley, California, opened by Alice Waters. The downstairs room serves a set menu that changes each day; the café upstairs opened in 1980.

orgs.name: 430 King's Road shop
orgs.summary: The London shop of Vivienne Westwood and Malcolm McLaren. It sold under the names Let It Rock, SEX and Seditionaries, and it dressed the first punk scene.

orgs.name: Nike, Inc.
orgs.summary: The sports shoe company that grew out of Blue Ribbon Sports. In 1985 it launched the signed Air Jordan 1.

orgs.name: Atari, Inc.
orgs.summary: The arcade and console company that made the first hit vector-display games.

orgs.name: Pentagram
orgs.summary: A design studio owned by its partners. It drew many wordmarks for companies and institutions.

orgs.name: SAP
orgs.summary: German software company, founded by five former IBM engineers. It makes SAP Fiori, the design system for its business software.

orgs.name: Global Tools
orgs.summary: A network of Italian radical groups and designers who ran a counter-school of workshops on the body, play and craft. It met for about two years.

moves.text: Radical architects and designers founded the network in Florence.
The network stopped its work.

orgs.name: Patagonia
orgs.summary: The outdoor clothes firm of Yvon Chouinard. It made pile and fleece jackets from 1979 that later became the core of gorpcore.

orgs.name: Giorgio Armani fashion house
orgs.summary: The Milan house that Giorgio Armani founded in 1975. It made the soft, plain suits that became the uniform of the 1980s office.

orgs.name: Microsoft
orgs.summary: US software company. It bought Mojang in 2014 for 2.5 billion dollars and put billions of dollars into OpenAI from 2019. Its design teams made the Metro and Fluent design systems.

orgs.name: New Topographics
orgs.summary: A show of landscape photography at George Eastman House. Its plain views of houses, roads and industry gave a movement its name.

orgs.name: Punk
orgs.summary: A fanzine of the New York punk scene, with hand-lettered pages and comics. It made the word punk a name for the music.

orgs.name: Apple
orgs.summary: US technology company known for consumer electronics, software and online services. It made the Aqua, iOS and Liquid Glass interface designs.

orgs.name: La Grande Cuisine minceur
orgs.summary: The cookbook of Michel Guérard on slimming haute cuisine, with Alain Coumont, published by Robert Laffont in 1976.

orgs.name: Sniffin' Glue
orgs.summary: A punk zine that Mark Perry typed, cut and photocopied. Its rough paste-up look became the model for punk print.

orgs.name: Heavy Metal
orgs.summary: A magazine of science fiction and fantasy comics. It printed airbrushed covers and smooth, dream-like painted worlds.

orgs.name: Brunello Cucinelli house
orgs.summary: The firm that Brunello Cucinelli began in 1978 with cashmere in colour. It makes fine, logo-free clothes in the village of Solomeo.

orgs.name: Omni
orgs.summary: A magazine of science and science fiction. Its painted covers showed hardware futures, chrome and airbrushed worlds.

orgs.name: Restaurant Bras
orgs.summary: The family restaurant of Michel Bras in the Aubrac, where he first made the gargouillou and built the plate as a landscape of plants.

orgs.name: Sundance Film Festival
orgs.summary: A festival of independent film. The Blair Witch Project and the iPhone feature Tangerine had their premieres here.

orgs.name: Memphis Group
orgs.summary: A collective of designers round Ettore Sottsass that showed bold laminate furniture and objects. Its first show in 1981 launched the Memphis style.

orgs.name: Stüssy
orgs.summary: The label that Shawn Stussy began in 1980 with printed T-shirts and shorts. It was one of the first labels of streetwear.

orgs.name: Venice Biennale of Architecture
orgs.summary: An architecture show that the Venice Biennale holds every two years. Its first edition built a street of postmodern facades, and later editions showed buildings made again from old structures.

orgs.name: MTV
orgs.summary: US cable channel for music video. It began on 1 August 1981 under Warner-Amex Satellite Entertainment.

orgs.name: Soviet paper architects
orgs.summary: A scene of young Moscow architects who drew impossible buildings for international competitions and could not build them. Their etchings made the Soviet paper dream known in the West.

moves.text: Young Moscow architects began to win international ideas competitions; they won fifty of them by 1989. Avvakumov gave the work the name paper architecture.
The Moscow Institute of Architecture showed Paper Architecture. Alma Mater.

orgs.name: Adobe
orgs.summary: A software company that makes Spectrum, the design system behind its products and experiences.

orgs.name: Dapper Dan's Boutique
orgs.summary: A boutique and workshop in Harlem. It made jackets, bags and other pieces printed with the logos of luxury houses, for musicians and sportsmen.

orgs.name: Jean Paul Gaultier fashion house
orgs.summary: The Paris house of Jean Paul Gaultier. The house showed the corset with a cone bra in 1984, and the corset became its mark.

orgs.name: Stone Island
orgs.summary: The label of Massimo Osti, launched in 1982. It tested new cloths and garment dyes on sport and military shapes, and it set the base of techwear.

orgs.name: Ultimate Play the Game
orgs.summary: A British studio whose isometric room engine set a look for home computer games.

orgs.name: Chinois on Main
orgs.summary: A restaurant in Santa Monica, California, opened by Wolfgang Puck and Barbara Lazaroff. It served French and Californian food with Chinese and Asian flavours.

orgs.name: Swatch factory and watch line
orgs.summary: The Swiss watch line that came out on 1 March 1983 in Zurich. It put a plastic quartz watch of few parts on the market as a fashion accessory.

orgs.name: Mondo 2000
orgs.summary: A glossy cyberculture magazine. It mixed virtual reality, hackers, rave and psychedelics in a dense, neon layout.

orgs.name: Macworld Expo
orgs.summary: A trade show for the Apple Macintosh. Apple showed new products and systems on its stage, among them the Aqua interface in January 2000.

orgs.name: Famitsu
orgs.summary: A Japanese weekly game magazine that reviews and previews games, from 8-bit to current hardware.

orgs.name: Square
orgs.summary: A Japanese game studio known for role-playing games with rich 16-bit pixel art and pre-rendered 3D rooms.

orgs.name: Cyan Worlds
orgs.place: Mead, Washington (in Spokane at the 1987 founding)
orgs.summary: An American studio that made Myst from pre-rendered still images.

orgs.name: LVMH
orgs.summary: French luxury group. Moët Hennessy and Louis Vuitton merged in 1987. Bernard Arnault took control in 1989. It owns Dior and, with Prada, bought Fendi in 1999.

orgs.name: South by Southwest
orgs.summary: A festival of music, film and media. Its 2005 film program showed the low-budget talk films that got the name mumblecore.

orgs.name: Deconstructivist Architecture
orgs.summary: A show at the Museum of Modern Art. It put seven architects together and gave the deconstructivist movement its name.

orgs.name: Nintendo Power
orgs.summary: A monthly magazine from Nintendo of America that printed maps, sprite art and screens of its games.

orgs.name: Electronic Gaming Monthly
orgs.summary: An American game magazine that covered the 16-bit console years with screens and reviews.

orgs.name: ACiD Productions
orgs.summary: An art group of ANSI artists. It released its work as monthly art packs for bulletin boards.

orgs.name: Blizzard Entertainment
orgs.summary: An American studio known for chunky, hand-painted fantasy worlds.

orgs.name: Epic Games
orgs.summary: An American studio and engine maker: the gritty HD shooters of the 2000s, then physically based Unreal Engine.

orgs.name: Unicode Consortium
orgs.summary: A non-profit group of software firms that keeps the Unicode text standard. It added emoji to the standard in 2010 and now votes on each new set.

orgs.name: Ray Gun
orgs.summary: An alternative rock magazine that David Carson art-directed. Its layered, broken type pages defined grunge typography.

orgs.name: Edge
orgs.summary: A British game magazine with a focus on design and art direction since the first polygon consoles.

orgs.name: Astrid y Gastón
orgs.summary: The restaurant of Gastón Acurio and Astrid Gutsche in Lima, which took Peruvian produce and ceviche into fine dining.

orgs.name: GeoCities
orgs.summary: A free host for personal home pages. Its pages used tiled backgrounds, pixel GIFs, counters and under-construction signs.

emblem.credit: The original uploader was 718 Bot at English Wikipedia

orgs.name: Vice
orgs.summary: A youth culture magazine. Its pages were full of direct-flash party and street photos.

orgs.name: Yahoo!
orgs.summary: A link directory that grew into a web portal with search, mail and news on one page.

orgs.name: Dogme 95
orgs.summary: A group of Danish directors who signed a set of rules for film making. They banned sets, added light and a score. The first Dogme films came in 1998.

statement.title: Vow of Chastity
statement.text: The directors vow to film on location with a handheld camera, in colour, with the real sound, with no special light (one lamp on the camera at most), no filter, no genre and no credit for the director.

moves.text: Von Trier and Vinterberg wrote the manifesto and the Vow of Chastity.
The first Dogme films came out: Festen and The Idiots.
The movement broke up.

orgs.name: Newgrounds
orgs.summary: A web site where users post Flash games and animations. It spread the look of Flash sites.

emblem.credit: The original uploader was GoMan195531 at English Wikipedia

orgs.name: The Fat Duck
orgs.summary: A restaurant in a village by the Thames; Heston Blumenthal built long tasting menus with low-temperature cooking, liquid nitrogen and play with memory.

orgs.name: The Iconfactory
orgs.summary: An icon design studio. It made pixel icons for early desktops and detailed, lit icons for Mac OS X and iOS.

orgs.name: Rhizome
orgs.summary: An online platform for new media art. It hosted a mailing list, an archive and the work of net artists.

orgs.name: Wallpaper*
orgs.summary: A magazine of design, interiors and travel. It published spare, minimal rooms and architecture.

orgs.name: Yahoo! Japan
orgs.summary: A Japanese web portal. Its home page packs news, links and services into many small text blocks, the model of the dense Japanese web.

orgs.name: Company 3
orgs.summary: A colour grading company that Stefan Sonnenfeld co-founded. Its grades for action films spread the teal and orange look.

orgs.name: Despair, Inc.
orgs.summary: A company that sells black-framed Demotivators posters, the print model of the demotivational poster.

orgs.name: eBoy
orgs.summary: A pixel art studio. It builds large isometric cities from small pixel objects.

orgs.name: Eleven Madison Park
orgs.summary: A restaurant on Madison Square in New York; under Daniel Humm it changed in 2021 to a tasting menu of plant-based food only, and put some animal products back in 2025.

orgs.name: Mugaritz
orgs.summary: A restaurant in the hills near San Sebastián and a research kitchen, where Andoni Luis Aduriz joins wild plants with odd texture and play.

orgs.name: Stora Enso
orgs.summary: A Finnish and Swedish forest company. It makes cross-laminated timber and glued beams for tall wood buildings.

orgs.name: 2channel
orgs.summary: A large anonymous Japanese text board. Its users spread text faces, and Futaba Channel, the model for 4chan, began in 2001 as a refuge for its users.

orgs.name: Salesforce
orgs.summary: US software company. Its UX team made the Lightning Design System, a CSS framework for Salesforce apps.

orgs.name: Dwell
orgs.summary: A magazine of modern homes. It shows lofts, prefabs and plain rooms of raw materials.

orgs.name: phpBB
orgs.summary: A free and open-source forum program, made by a development team. Its default theme, subSilver, gave many later forum themes their look.

orgs.name: Smilebit
orgs.summary: A Sega studio that made Jet Set Radio, an early cel-shaded 3D game.

orgs.name: Spanx
orgs.summary: A maker of shapewear that Sara Blakely founded in Atlanta in 2000. Its first product was a pair of footless control-top tights.

orgs.name: Atlassian
orgs.summary: Australian software company that Mike Cannon-Brookes and Scott Farquhar founded. It makes the Atlassian Design System.

orgs.name: Dutch Design Week
orgs.summary: A yearly design festival in Eindhoven. Young designers show new work there, and several of them showed 3D-printed ceramics in the 2010s.

orgs.name: 4chan
orgs.summary: An anonymous image board. In 2019 a post of an empty yellow room on its paranormal board began the Backrooms and the liminal spaces look.

orgs.name: Myspace
orgs.summary: A social network of profile pages. Users posted flash digicam photos and filled their pages with glitter, gloss and custom code.

orgs.name: Noma
orgs.summary: A restaurant in a former warehouse in Copenhagen; its seasonal tasting menu and its fermentation lab set the New Nordic kitchen.

orgs.name: Tesla Motors
orgs.summary: The car maker that started in 2003. Its Model S of 2012 had a smooth body, no grille and one large screen in the dashboard.

orgs.name: Facebook
orgs.summary: A social network. Small image groups on it started Health Goth in 2013.

orgs.name: ustwo
orgs.summary: A British digital studio whose games team made Monument Valley.

orgs.name: Vimeo
orgs.summary: A video site that film makers use to show their work. Cinematic drone and FPV films spread from it.

orgs.name: Web 2.0 Conference
orgs.summary: A conference of web companies that spread the term Web 2.0 and its ideas of user-made content.

orgs.name: Alinea
orgs.summary: A restaurant of Grant Achatz in Chicago that serves a tasting menu of exact modernist methods, with scent, edible balloons and theatrical service.

orgs.name: Behance
orgs.summary: A web site where designers post portfolios of projects. Concept work for interfaces, logos and illustration spreads from it.

orgs.name: Reddit
orgs.summary: A forum site of topic groups. The groups on Weirdcore and Liminalspace spread the images of empty, strange places.

orgs.name: YouTube
orgs.summary: A web site where people post video. The daily vlog grew here, and it became the main home of the music video.

orgs.name: Shopify
orgs.summary: Canadian e-commerce company. It makes the Polaris design system for its admin and for partner apps.

orgs.name: Smashing Magazine
orgs.summary: An online magazine for web designers and developers. Its tutorials and free icon sets spread the glossy Web 2.0 look and then the flat look.

orgs.name: Super Normal exhibition
orgs.summary: A show of everyday objects chosen by Jasper Morrison and Naoto Fukasawa. It set out the idea of the Super Normal object: a plain thing that works well and needs no comment.

orgs.name: The Row
orgs.summary: A New York house, opened in 2006 by Mary-Kate and Ashley Olsen. It makes plain clothes and leather goods with no logo.

orgs.name: Twitter
orgs.summary: A site of short public posts. Its post card is the frame of the tweet screenshot meme, and many label memes spread here.

orgs.name: Bandcamp
orgs.summary: A web site where musicians sell music. Vaporwave and synthwave artists released their albums and cover art there.

orgs.name: GitHub
orgs.summary: A web site where developers host code. Its own dark interface and the editor themes and terminal tools that it hosts set the look of software for engineers.

orgs.name: SoundCloud
orgs.summary: A site where people post music. The digicore and hyperpop scenes shared tracks and cover art here.

orgs.name: Tumblr
orgs.summary: A microblog site of reblogged images. Vaporwave and other net aesthetics grew in its image feeds.

orgs.name: App Store
orgs.summary: The store of Apple for iPhone and iPad apps. Apps and their icons follow the platform look of each era, from leather and glass to flat colour and Liquid Glass, and premium mobile games with a clean art style found a large public there.

orgs.name: Central
orgs.summary: The restaurant of Virgilio Martínez in Lima, with a menu that goes by altitude from the sea to the high Andes.

orgs.name: Google Play
orgs.summary: The app store of Android. After 2014 its apps took the cards, colour and shadows of Material Design.

orgs.name: Awwwards
orgs.summary: A web site that gives awards to web design. Designers post sites there, and its daily picks spread trends of the expressive web.

orgs.name: Dribbble
orgs.summary: A web site where designers post small shots of interface work. Several interface trends, neumorphism among them, spread from shots that were posted there.

orgs.name: Hato Press
orgs.summary: A London publisher that prints books and zines on the risograph and teaches the method in workshops.

orgs.name: Kickstarter
orgs.summary: The crowd-funding site where Pebble sold its first smartwatch to backers in 2012, a year before the big makers entered the market.

orgs.name: Maido
orgs.summary: The Nikkei restaurant of Mitsuharu Tsumura in Lima, where Japanese technique meets the chillies, fish and tubers of Peru.

orgs.name: Mojang Studios
orgs.summary: A Swedish studio that makes Minecraft.

orgs.name: Museum Brandhorst
orgs.summary: An art museum in Munich that opened in 2009. Its facade has 36,000 ceramic rods in 23 colours, hung on rails in front of the wall.

orgs.name: Uber
orgs.summary: A technology company that makes the Base design system and its React implementation, Base Web.

orgs.name: Google Fonts
orgs.summary: A free library of web fonts and icons. It serves the Material Symbols icon font and many open sans and serif families.

orgs.name: Instagram
orgs.summary: A photo and video app. Home and food images spread on it, and it carried trends such as dopamine decor and the film grain look.

orgs.name: Pinterest
orgs.summary: A web site where people pin images to boards. Its boards of rooms, crafts and mood images spread home and craft styles.

emblem.credit: Grilli Type, Pinterest (Andreas Helin, Michelle Van Houten and Simon Blockley) and MadeThought

orgs.name: The Noun Project
orgs.summary: A web site that collects simple symbols from designers around the world. Its library is a large source of flat and glyph icons.

orgs.name: iMessage
orgs.summary: The Apple messaging service. Animoji and Memoji came to it in 2017 and 2018 as face-tracked 3D emoji.

orgs.name: Government Digital Service
